# Survey Response Timing Analysis

Import tidyverse library

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
```

First we read the csv into a df and take a look

```{r}
response_timing_data <- read.csv("../data/response-timing.csv")
response_timing_data
```

Removing the year part of the date

```{r}
response_timing_data <- response_timing_data %>% 
  mutate(date = str_sub(date, start = 6, end = 10)) %>%
  mutate(class_day = date %in% c("09-24", "09-29", "10-01"))
```

Now let's plot this data

```{r}
ggplot(response_timing_data, aes(x = date, y = n, fill = class_day)) + 
  geom_col()

ggsave("../results/response_timing_bar_chart_class_day_color.png", width = 6, height = 4, units = "in", dpi = 300)
```

# Analysis: Class Day vs. Non-Class Day Hypothesis Test

Looking at the data we hypothesize 9/24 and 9/29 are the spikes because they were class days and people were reminded to complete the survey. Class days occurred on 9/24, 9/29, and 10/1. To test this, we will perform a one-sided permutation test.

- Null hypothesis: number of surveys completed on a given day is independent of whether the day is a class day
- Alternative hypothesis: the day being a class day is positively associated with number of surveys completed
- Test statistic: mean completion on class days - mean completion on non-class days
- Null distribution: test statistic computed for every possible assignment of the 3 class-day labels to the 13 days (13 choose 3)
- P-value: how often is this test-statistic larger than or equal to the observed result

*Since we formed the hypothesis by looking at the data, the reported p-value will likely overstate the significance of the results. Thus, we will not set a significance level and make a reject/fail to reject decision based on the reported p-value. We are simply performing this test as an exploratory, descriptive analysis. Further, since this analysis is non-experimental, it can only suggest correlation, not causation.*

```{r}
y <- response_timing_data$n
is_class <- response_timing_data$class_day

# Calculate observed test statistic
observed_test_statistic <- mean(y[is_class]) - mean(y[!is_class])

# Calculate null distribution: for each possible assignment of class days, calculate test statistic
null_dist <- combn(length(y), sum(is_class), \(idx) mean(y[idx]) - mean(y[-idx]))

# Plot histogram of null distribution and mark observed test statistic
ggplot(tibble(diff = null_dist), aes(diff)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = observed_test_statistic, color = "red") + 
  labs(title = "Permutation null distribution",
     x = "Mean class day surveys completed - mean non-class day surveys completed",
     y = "Count") + 
  annotate("text", x = observed_test_statistic, y = Inf,
         label = paste("Observed =", round(observed_test_statistic, 2)),
         vjust = 1.5, hjust = -0.1, color = "red") +
  annotate("text", x =8, y = 5, label = paste("P-value =", round(mean(null_dist >= observed_test_statistic), 2)), color = "black")

ggsave("../results/response_timing_permutation_null_distribution.png", width = 6, height = 4, units = "in", dpi = 300)
```
